claims.text: The starting FeNiCrCoCu nanoparticles are solid and nominally single-phase.
Local composition fluctuations at nanoparticle surfaces and grain boundaries govern the onset of premelting.
Interfacial composition fluctuations reduce the local melting temperature.
Melting initiates at surfaces and grain boundaries and progresses inward through multiple steps.
Rapid in situ TEM heating can provide time-resolved observation of structural changes in heated nanoparticles.
Approximately 1600 K is near or above the relevant bulk melting range or solidus for FeNiCrCoCu.
The proposed experiment applies to size-selected nanoparticles approximately 5–50 nm in diameter.
Heating under TEM vacuum can deplete selected alloy constituents and alter nanoparticle composition.
Composition depletion or enrichment occurs specifically at FeNiCrCoCu surfaces and grain boundaries.
Thermally driven surface and grain-boundary diffusion produces localized enrichment of lower-melting constituents.
Localized enrichment of lower-melting constituents lowers the effective local melting point and creates a partial liquid.
The partial liquid region expands inward as temperature increases.
Premelting will first produce diffraction peak broadening or splitting associated with near-surface regions.
Progressive melting will produce localized liquid-like diffuse scattering.
Complete melting will occur below or across the nominal bulk melting point rather than only above it.
Slower heating or greater compositional uniformity will cause more spatially uniform melting at a temperature closer to the bulk solidus.
The proposed mechanism may cease to apply at extreme particle sizes or when processing eliminates or freezes compositional gradients.
The temperature offset for initial melting depends strongly on particle size, heating rate, and local stoichiometry.
Uniform melting throughout the particle at a single temperature, without localized early melting at surfaces or boundaries, would falsify the hypothesis.
